transcript.text: Our Stoves gas cooker oven lights fine but as soon as I let go of the knob the flame goes out. Hob burners all fine. It's a Richmond something, freestanding. Is this a DIY job?

# Almost Certainly the Thermocouple (Flame Failure Device)

The thermocouple is a small metal probe that sits in the oven burner flame. When it's hot, it generates a tiny current that holds the gas valve open. When you let go of the knob and the flame dies, the valve isn't getting that signal. Usually the thermocouple is worn, dirty, out of position, or loose. Less often the magnet unit in the valve/thermostat has failed.

Since the hob is fine, your gas supply is fine. It's isolated to the oven circuit.

## Free Things to Try First

1. Hold the knob in longer. Keep it pressed for a full 15–20 seconds after ignition. Thermocouples get sluggish with age, and this sometimes gets you by.
2. Check the flame is touching the probe. The thermocouple tip (a small rod near the burner, usually at the back or side of the oven floor once you lift the base panel) should sit right in the flame. If it's been knocked aside, gently ease it back.
3. Clean the tip. With the oven cold and off, lightly rub the tip with fine wire wool or emery cloth to remove carbon or grease buildup.

## Is Replacing It DIY?

Legally (UK): The Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations require anyone working on gas fittings to be competent. For paid work they must be Gas Safe registered. DIY isn't strictly banned, but if something goes wrong you're liable, and it may affect your home insurance.

Practically: On most cookers, the thermocouple's far end screws into the oven thermostat/valve's magnet unit, which doesn't carry gas itself. So it's one of the more approachable jobs. But it does mean pulling the cooker out, removing panels, and working right next to the gas valve. Many people do it themselves; many sensibly don't.

My honest take: If you're handy and careful, a thermocouple swap is within reach. If you're not confident around gas components, or the problem turns out to be the valve/thermostat rather than the thermocouple, call a Gas Safe engineer. Check an engineer's registration at gassaferegister.co.uk.

## If You Go Ahead

• Find your exact model number. On Stoves Richmond cookers, the rating plate is usually inside the storage drawer area or on the oven door frame. "Richmond" covers many variants (550, 600, 900, etc.), so you need the exact number to get the right part.
• Cost: A genuine thermocouple is typically around £10–£30. An engineer will likely charge £80–£150 including the part.
• Make sure the cooker is cold and the gas is isolated before you start.
• Tighten the thermocouple nut at the valve end firmly but don't overtighten. Finger tight plus about a quarter turn is the usual guidance.
• Afterwards, check the oven lights, stays lit after you release the knob, and goes out properly when switched off.

## Safety

If you ever smell gas, turn it off at the meter, open windows, don't operate any electrical switches, and call the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999 (free, 24/7).

If you can find the full model number, I can help you track down the right part.

Thank you. I tried holding the knob in for 15, 20 and even 30 seconds and it still goes out when I let go. I'm not comfortable lifting the oven base panel or taking anything apart on a gas cooker. I only smell gas briefly while I'm trying to light it, and it clears quickly. The CO alarm in the kitchen hasn't gone off. Is there anything else I can check from the outside?

Good that you've ruled out the "hold it longer" fix, and that you're not opening panels. Here's what you can safely check from the outside.

## First, a Quick Safety Note

• A brief whiff while lighting is normal. Some gas escapes before it catches.
• Don't keep making repeated attempts. Each one releases a little unburnt gas into the oven. If you try again, leave the oven door open and wait a few minutes between attempts.
• If you ever smell gas that doesn't clear, turn the knob off, don't use switches or flames, open windows, and call the National Gas Emergency line on 0800 111 999 (free, 24/7).

## Things to Check Without Taking Anything Apart

1. The clock/timer (if your cooker has one). On many Stoves cookers with an electronic timer, the oven won't stay on if the clock is flashing (often after a power cut) or is set to an automatic cooking mode. Check that it shows the correct time and is set to manual, not "auto". Your user manual will show how; Stoves manuals are free to download online if you've lost yours.
2. Door open while lighting. Some models are designed to be lit with the door open. Check your manual.
3. The knob is pushing in fully. If it's cracked, loose, or feels like it doesn't depress as far as it used to, it may not be engaging the valve properly. Compare it with how firmly the hob knobs press in.
4. Look at the flame through the oven floor openings (no dismantling). With the door open, does the flame look steady, blue, and lit along the burner? A weak, yellow, or patchy flame is useful information for an engineer.
5. Draughts. A nearby open window or fan blowing across the cooker can occasionally affect a weak flame.

## If None of That Helps

It's most likely the thermocouple, and that's a job for a Gas Safe registered engineer. It's usually a fairly quick, inexpensive repair.

To speed things up, find the model and serial number before you call. On Stoves cookers this is usually on a rating plate inside the oven door frame or behind the storage drawer, so you won't need tools. The engineer can then bring the right part, potentially fixing it in one visit.
